sources.citation: Lewis, Gilbert. 2021. Pandora's Box: Ethnography and the Comparison of Medical Beliefs. The 1979 Lewis Henry Morgan Lectures. Chicago: HAU Books. xii+300 pp. ISBN 978-1-912808-36-6 (open access; OAPEN handle 20.500.12657/48466).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No phonology content. The only language remarks are sociolinguistic (ch. 1, pp. 14-16): the Gnau-speaking villages lie behind Anguganak Bluff; 'Within this circle, ten different languages were spoken in forty-two villages. Gnau speakers are likely to know one neighboring language in addition to their own and the contact language of Tok Pisin.' Occasional Gnau words are cited (e.g. biape 'palm-leaf spathe') without any transcription or pronunciation note; the appendix is a translated transcript of a healing rite whose song words are 'in a language of the spirit world'.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 page for gnau1240; Wikipedia 'Gnau language'; Encyclopedia of World Cultures (Oceania) 'Gnau' entry (N. Gratton) via encyclopedia.com; Carrington 1996, A linguistic bibliography of the New Guinea area (search-inside snippet).
sources.note: Glottolog lists no descriptive reference (only Laycock 1973 for classification). Wikipedia has no phonology section. Encyclopedia entry gives only affiliation (Wapei family) and Tok Pisin bilingualism. Carrington 1996 entries for Gnau: Lewis 1968-69 w/l, Lewis 1974, Lewis 1975. Nothing on stress anywhere.
